steps.body: The three angles inside ANY triangle always add up to **180°**. Know two of them and you can find the third by subtracting from 180. This holds for every triangle, no matter its shape.

widget.prompt: Drag corner C to reshape the triangle until angle A reads 40°. Watch all three readouts — and especially their total — the whole way.
widget.successFeedback: Angle A is 40°. Now look at what happened while you were dragging: every angle changed, and the total never did — it read 180° at every single position. That is why knowing two angles fixes the third: the two you know plus the one you don't must fill exactly 180°, so the third is whatever is left over.
widget.targetFeedback: Not 40° at corner A yet. Drag C further from A to open that angle, closer to narrow it — and keep an eye on the total as you do.
widget.invariantFeedback: Reshape the triangle a few more times first. One position cannot show you that the sum is fixed; watching it survive several different triangles is the entire point.

predict.prompt: Two angles are set at 40° and 60°. Is the third angle FORCED?
predict.reveal: 180° is every triangle's fixed budget: 40 + 60 spends 100, leaving exactly 80 — no freedom left. Two angles always determine the third, which is why matching two angles will be enough for similarity.

steps.body: This works even for right triangles. A right triangle has one 90° angle, so the other two must add to 90°. If one of them is 35°, the last is 90 − 35 = 55°.

explanationVariants: With a 90° and a 35° angle, the third is 180 − 90 − 35 = 55°.

widget.prompt: A right triangle has a 90° angle and a 35° angle. What is the third angle?
All three angles of a triangle are equal. What is each one, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: Three EQUAL angles summing to 180° are each 180 ÷ 3 = 60°, not 90°.
That's the total of all three — each one is 180 ÷ 3 = 60°.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Three equal angles sum to 180°, so each is 180 ÷ 3 = 60°.

widget.prompt: A triangle has angles of 25° and 115°. What is the third?

commonErrors.feedback: The three add to 180° — subtract both: 180 − 25 − 115 = 40°.

explanationVariants: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles: 50 + 60 = 110°.
The exterior angle equals the two far interior angles added: 110°.

widget.prompt: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two far (remote) interior angles. If those are 50° and 60°, what is the exterior angle?

commonErrors.feedback: Add the two remote angles: 50 + 60 = 110°, don't subtract.
The exterior angle is the SUM: 50 + 60 = 110°.

widget.fallbackFeedback: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles: 50 + 60 = 110°.

steps.body: Combine the angle sum with a straight line.
explanationVariants: Third interior angle: 180 − 70 − 60 = 50°. The exterior angle beside it: 180 − 50 = 130° (or add the remotes 70 + 60 = 130°).
Interior third is 50°; its exterior angle is 130°.

widget.prompt: A triangle has angles 70° and 60°. What is the EXTERIOR angle at the third corner?

commonErrors.feedback: That's the interior third angle — its EXTERIOR angle is 180 − 50 = 130°.
The exterior angle equals the two remote interiors: 70 + 60 = 130°, not 110°.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The third interior angle is 180 − 70 − 60 = 50°, so the exterior angle is 180 − 50 = 130° (= 70 + 60).

hints: First find the third interior angle: 180 − 70 − 60.
That gives 50°. The exterior angle is on a straight line with it.
Exterior = 180 − 50 = 130° — which also equals the two remote angles, 70 + 60.

steps.body: A triangle's three angles always sum to 180°, and an exterior angle equals the two remote interior angles.
takeaways: The three interior angles of any triangle sum to 180°.
Find a missing angle by subtracting the known ones from 180.
An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.
